Adding an `argument-hint` that describes the situations and file types in which the skill applies.

rationale.correct: Skills are triggered by Claude matching the ongoing conversation and task against the skill's description — unlike a slash command, which requires the user to explicitly type it. A clear, specific description that states what the skill does and when it applies is what drives automatic invocation.

distractors.B: `disable-model-invocation: true` does the opposite of what's wanted here — it disables automatic triggering, forcing the skill to be invoked manually only.
distractors.C: `context: fork` controls whether the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context, not whether or when it gets invoked.
distractors.D: `argument-hint` only affects the hint shown when a user manually invokes the skill as a slash command; it has no bearing on automatic invocation.

scenario: A `/deploy` slash command needs to accept an environment name at invocation time, e.g. `/deploy staging`, and use that value inside the command's own instructions.
stem: What is the correct mechanism for this?

options.text: Reference `$ARGUMENTS` in the command's markdown body; Claude Code substitutes the text typed after the command name.
Hard-code every possible environment name as a separate command (`/deploy-staging`, `/deploy-production`, etc.).
Use `argument-hint` alone in the frontmatter, since it both documents the argument and supplies its value.
Ask the user to paste the environment name into the chat separately after invoking `/deploy` with no arguments.

rationale.correct: Slash commands support an argument placeholder in their body that Claude Code fills in with whatever text follows the command name at invocation — that's the direct mechanism for passing a value like an environment name into the command's own instructions.

distractors.B: Creating a separate command per possible value doesn't scale and duplicates the command's logic for no reason.
distractors.C: `argument-hint` only supplies documentation text shown to the user about what to provide; it does not itself carry the actual value through to the command body.
distractors.D: Requiring a separate follow-up message defeats the purpose of a single-invocation command that already supports passing arguments directly.

scenario: A `full-audit` skill needs to run a lengthy, verbose codebase scan (best isolated in its own context) and then hand a concise summary to the main conversation for the developer to act on.
stem: Which configuration best fits this?

options.text: `context: fork`, so the verbose scan runs in an isolated sub-agent context and returns only a concise summary.
`allowed-tools` restricted to file-write tools only, since the skill's job is fundamentally about producing output.
`argument-hint` describing the scan's scope, since the declared scope determines where and how the skill's work runs.
No special configuration — skills already run their work in an isolated context by default, so the output stays separate.

rationale.correct: `context: fork` is exactly the mechanism for isolating a skill's verbose internal work in its own sub-agent context while only a concise result returns to the main conversation — matching both stated needs (isolation for the scan, a clean summary for the developer).

distractors.B: `allowed-tools` restricts which tools the skill may call; it doesn't isolate where its context/output lives.
distractors.C: `argument-hint` only documents expected invocation arguments; it has no effect on context isolation.
distractors.D: Skills don't isolate their context by default — `context: fork` is an explicit opt-in for exactly this need.

scenario: Configuration files matching *.config.ts are scattered across many packages in a repository, and the team wants Claude to automatically apply one convention to all of them regardless of directory.
stem: What is the most maintainable approach?

options.text: Create a .claude/rules/ file with YAML frontmatter whose paths glob is **/*.config.ts.
Place a CLAUDE.md in each package directory describing the convention.
Create a skill developers invoke manually when editing config files.
Add one large section to the root CLAUDE.md and rely on Claude to infer when it applies.

rationale.correct: Glob-scoped rules in .claude/rules/ apply automatically by file pattern across any directory, which is exactly what's needed for files scattered across packages.

distractors.B: A CLAUDE.md per package is directory-bound and requires duplicating and maintaining the convention in every package.
distractors.C: A manually invoked skill requires developers to remember to run it — it isn't automatic.
distractors.D: Relying on inference from one large, monolithic root file is unreliable compared to an explicit glob-scoped rule.

scenario: `.claude/rules/general-style.md` (`paths: ["**/*.ts"]`) says 'always use `async/await`, never raw Promises.' `.claude/rules/legacy-adapter.md` (`paths: ["src/adapters/legacy/**/*.ts"]`) says 'this directory intentionally uses raw `.then()` chains for compatibility with an older build target — do not convert to async/await here.'
stem: When editing a file inside `src/adapters/legacy/`, what should happen?

options.text: Both rules load, since the file matches both globs, and the narrower legacy-adapter rule governs this directory.
Only the general-style rule applies, since it was created first and sets the project-wide default for TypeScript.
Both rules cancel each other out, so no style guidance applies in that directory at all and Claude uses its own defaults.
Claude should refuse to edit the file until the conflict is manually resolved by deleting one rule.

rationale.correct: Path-scoped rules can legitimately express an exception for a narrower path, and a well-written narrower rule (like the legacy-adapter one) is written to explicitly carve out that exception. Both rules load because the file matches both globs — that is expected — and the more specific, purpose-written guidance for that exact directory is the one that should govern code in it.

distractors.B: Creation order isn't the mechanism that determines precedence between path-scoped rules; specificity and intent are.
distractors.C: Rules don't cancel each other by being simultaneously present; both are simply part of the context loaded for that file.
distractors.D: Refusing to edit isn't warranted — this is a normal, intentional exception pattern, not an unresolvable conflict.

scenario: A team wants a rule to apply to every TypeScript file in the repository except those under `src/generated/`, which is auto-generated code no one should hand-edit or apply style conventions to.
stem: What is the most direct way to express this scope in the rule's frontmatter?

options.text: Use a `paths` include like `**/*.ts` paired with an exclusion such as `!src/generated/**/*.ts` (or equivalent negative glob).
List every non-generated directory individually in `paths`, so `src/generated/` is simply never mentioned and stays out of scope.
There is no way to exclude a subdirectory; the rule must apply repo-wide or not at all, so generated files are included.
Add a comment inside the `src/generated/` files asking Claude to ignore the rule whenever it edits them.

rationale.correct: A broad include pattern paired with an explicit exclusion for the generated directory directly expresses 'everywhere except here,' carving generated code out explicitly — both clearer and far less brittle than manually enumerating every directory that isn't excluded.

distractors.B: Manually listing every non-generated directory is brittle — it silently stops covering any new directory added later unless someone remembers to update the list.
distractors.C: Path-scoping mechanisms generally support exclusion patterns; claiming it's impossible undersells the tooling.
distractors.D: An in-file comment isn't a supported activation mechanism for rules; scoping is controlled by frontmatter `paths`, not comments inside individual files.

scenario: A `.claude/rules/security-baseline.md` file has no `paths` field in its frontmatter at all, while every other rule in the project specifies one.
stem: When does this rule load into context?

options.text: On every request, regardless of which file is being edited, since omitting `paths` makes it always-loaded context.
Never, since a rule without a `paths` field is invalid and silently ignored by the rules loader.
Only when editing files directly inside `.claude/rules/`, since without `paths` the rule falls back to its own location.
Only on the first request of a session, after which it is dropped to save context.

rationale.correct: The `paths` field is what makes a rule conditionally activate for matching files; omitting it removes that condition entirely, so the rule behaves as always-loaded context rather than being triggered by a specific file type or location.

distractors.B: A missing `paths` field doesn't invalidate the rule; it changes its activation from conditional to unconditional.
distractors.C: The rule's own file location inside `.claude/rules/` isn't what its `paths` field (or lack of one) scopes — that field scopes which edited files trigger it.
distractors.D: There's no such per-session-first-request-only behavior; an always-loaded rule stays loaded for the whole session.

scenario: A stack trace points to a single function, and the proposed fix is a one-line guard clause. However, the same function is called from three different call sites, each of which needs a different fallback value when the guard triggers.
stem: Does this remain a direct-execution case, or does it warrant plan mode?

options.text: It's still direct execution — one function, one file, so complexity is inherently low regardless of caller behavior.
It warrants at least a brief planning step, since the three different fallback behaviors are a design decision.
It should always be plan mode, since any change with more than one caller is by definition a multi-file, architectural change.
It should be skipped entirely and left as a known issue, since it's now too complicated for a quick fix.

rationale.correct: The presence of a genuine design decision — three call sites needing different fallback behavior — is what determines the mode, not merely how many files or lines are touched. A brief planning step to decide each fallback is warranted even though the change footprint is still small.

distractors.A: File count alone doesn't capture the complexity here; the decision about differing fallback values is the actual driver.
distractors.C: Multiple callers alone doesn't make something architectural; the deciding factor is whether there's a genuine unresolved design choice, which is present here but wouldn't be in every multi-caller case.
distractors.D: The complexity is a design decision to resolve, not a reason to defer the fix indefinitely.

scenario: A migration touches 45 files across three distinct modules, each with different usage patterns of the deprecated library.
stem: What is the most effective way to structure the planning itself?

options.text: One single plan-mode pass covering all 45 files uniformly, since they all involve the same underlying migration.
A plan-mode pass per module, since each module's usage patterns may call for different migration steps.
Skip planning for two of the three modules since they are smaller, and only plan the largest one.
Plan once for the first module encountered, then apply that exact plan verbatim to the other two without further analysis.

rationale.correct: Different usage patterns per module mean the specific migration steps may genuinely differ even though the overall goal (replace the deprecated library) is shared; planning each module lets those real differences surface before code changes, rather than assuming one plan fits all three.

distractors.A: A single uniform pass risks missing module-specific usage differences that call for different specific steps.
distractors.C: Skipping planning for modules just because they're smaller ignores that usage-pattern differences, not size, are what drive the need to plan.
distractors.D: Applying one module's plan verbatim to others assumes their usage patterns match, which the scenario says they don't.

scenario: You enter plan mode to investigate what looked like a broad refactor touching 30 files. Ten minutes into the investigation, it becomes clear that 28 of those files just need an identical one-line import path update, and the remaining 2 need no changes at all — there's no real architectural decision left to make.
stem: What should you do?

options.text: Exit plan mode and switch to direct execution, since the remaining work is a simple, mechanical change.
Continue in plan mode regardless, since the task was originally scoped and approved as a 30-file change.
Abandon the task entirely, since the original plan-mode framing turned out to be wrong.
Restart the investigation from scratch in direct execution mode without carrying over what you just learned.

rationale.correct: Plan mode is a tool for situations with real design decisions or scale-driven complexity — once the investigation itself reveals the actual work is simple and mechanical with no remaining decisions, continuing to plan adds process without benefit; switching to direct execution matches the now-understood reality of the task.

distractors.B: Sticking rigidly to the original framing ignores what the investigation itself just revealed about the task's true nature.
distractors.C: A task simplifying under investigation is a good outcome, not a reason to abandon it.
distractors.D: Discarding what you just learned and starting over forces you to rediscover information you already have.

scenario: You begin direct execution on what looked like a single-file bug fix. Partway through, you discover the root cause actually requires changing a shared interface used by 12 other call sites, each with different, non-obvious compatibility requirements.
stem: What should you do?

options.text: Stop and switch to plan mode, since the fix has become a multi-call-site interface change with real design implications.
Continue direct execution to the end regardless, since you already started that way.
Revert all changes and wait for someone else to re-scope the task before touching it again.
Silently make the 12 call sites work by adding special-case handling for each, without stepping back to reconsider the overall approach.

rationale.correct: The task's real shape only became clear mid-execution — it's now a multi-site change with real compatibility tradeoffs, exactly the kind of situation plan mode is for. Switching modes when the task's true complexity is discovered mid-stream is the same principle as choosing plan mode upfront, just triggered later.

distractors.B: Continuing on the original, now-outdated assumption ignores real complexity that just surfaced.
distractors.C: Reverting and waiting is more disruptive than simply switching modes now that you have direct, first-hand knowledge of what the task actually requires.
distractors.D: Bolting on 12 special cases without stepping back to plan risks an inconsistent, hard-to-maintain patchwork instead of a coherent fix.

scenario: You provided two clear input/output examples for a normalize_address helper, and Claude's output now matches both examples exactly. On a third, unseen input with a format neither example covered, the transformation is unpredictable.
stem: What should you do next?

options.text: Add a third example covering a case near the one that failed, since more examples always resolve any remaining ambiguity.
Give up on the transformation as too ambiguous to specify.
Use the interview pattern so Claude surfaces the edge cases and formatting rules it's still uncertain about.
Lower the temperature, since the inconsistency is a randomness problem in sampling, not a gap in how the transformation was specified.

rationale.correct: Two examples successfully pinned down the cases they cover but don't necessarily generalize to unseen formats — that's a sign of an underlying rule that hasn't been made explicit, which is exactly what the interview pattern surfaces by having Claude ask about the specific gaps rather than guessing.

distractors.A: More examples can help, but only if they target the actual gap; a scattershot approach doesn't guarantee covering the next unseen case any better than the last two did.
distractors.B: Genuinely specifiable problems shouldn't be abandoned; the interview pattern is designed for exactly this kind of unresolved ambiguity.
distractors.D: Temperature affects sampling variability, not whether the underlying transformation rule has been adequately communicated.

scenario: A developer already has a fairly detailed written spec for a caching layer, covering invalidation and cache-stampede handling, but is unsure whether anything domain-specific is still missing.
stem: Is the interview pattern still the right technique here, given the spec is already fairly thorough?

options.text: No — since a written spec already covers invalidation and stampede handling, the interview pattern is redundant and should be skipped.
Yes — even a thorough spec can miss domain considerations its author never thought to write down, which interviewing surfaces.
No — the interview pattern is meant for greenfield work where no spec exists yet, not for refining a spec that's already written.
Yes — the interview pattern should replace the written spec entirely, so the requirements come from Claude's questions instead.

rationale.correct: A written spec captures what the author already thought to specify; it does not guarantee coverage of considerations the author didn't anticipate. The interview pattern's value is precisely in surfacing those unknown unknowns, which a thorough-but-still-authored spec doesn't rule out.

distractors.A: A spec existing doesn't mean it's complete; the interview pattern targets exactly the gap a self-authored spec can't self-diagnose.
distractors.C: The technique isn't gated on the absence of any spec — it complements one, testing it against considerations the author may have missed.
distractors.D: The interview pattern surfaces gaps in a spec; it doesn't need to replace a spec that's otherwise doing useful work.

scenario: A review surfaces three issues in a data pipeline: (1) a retry count that's hard-coded instead of configurable, (2) a race condition where two issues — a shared counter increment and a missing lock — jointly cause corrupted totals, and (3) the missing lock also independently causes a rare deadlock unrelated to the counter.
stem: How should these be grouped for the fix instructions?

options.text: All three in one message, since they all touch the same file.

The counter-increment and missing-lock issues together in one message (since they jointly cause the corruption), the hard-coded retry count as a separate, independent message; the deadlock should be folded into whichever message is sent first.

The counter-increment and missing-lock issues together in one message; the hard-coded retry count separately; the deadlock addressed together with the missing lock, since both stem from the same missing-lock root cause.
Each issue in its own separate message, since batching risks confusing the model regardless of whether issues interact.

rationale.correct: The counter/lock pair interacts and should be fixed jointly so the model reasons about them together. The retry count is unrelated and can be handled separately. The deadlock shares its root cause (the missing lock) with the corruption issue, so it belongs in that same message rather than being arbitrarily attached to whichever message happens to go first.

distractors.A: Grouping by file rather than by actual interaction ignores that the retry count doesn't interact with the other two at all.
distractors.B: Folding the deadlock into 'whichever message is sent first' is arbitrary; it belongs specifically with the missing-lock fix since they share a root cause, not with an unrelated batch by convenience.
distractors.D: Splitting every issue into its own message loses the benefit of joint reasoning for the counter/lock pair, which genuinely interact.

scenario: You're building a `normalize_phone_number` helper. Two problems have come up: (1) Claude's output format for the country code varies inconsistently across runs on the same kind of input, and (2) you're not sure what edge cases exist for numbers from countries with unusual formatting rules you're unfamiliar with.
stem: Which combination of techniques best addresses both problems?

options.text: Concrete input/output examples for the inconsistent country-code formatting, plus the interview pattern to surface unfamiliar-country edge cases.
Test-driven iteration alone, since writing tests first will automatically surface both the formatting inconsistency and the unfamiliar edge cases.
One large upfront specification covering every case you can currently think of, applied to both the formatting and edge-case problems.
The interview pattern alone for both problems, since it always identifies inconsistent output formatting as well as missing edge cases.

rationale.correct: These are two different kinds of gaps needing two different techniques: examples are the direct fix for output that's interpreted inconsistently from prose, while the interview pattern is specifically suited to surfacing considerations in an unfamiliar domain that you wouldn't have thought to specify yourself.

distractors.B: Test-driven iteration verifies against tests you write; it doesn't by itself surface edge cases in a domain you don't understand well enough to write tests for yet.
distractors.C: A specification is limited to what you already know to include — it can't cover edge cases in formatting rules you're not aware of.
distractors.D: The interview pattern targets unknown-unknowns, not inconsistent output formatting, which examples handle more directly.

scenario: A CI job already runs claude -p "Review this PR", yet the job still occasionally hangs on certain PRs.
stem: Given that -p is already correctly used, what is the most likely remaining cause of the hang?

options.text: -p doesn't actually prevent interactive prompts in all cases, so the fix is to abandon it and find another flag that fully suppresses them.
A tool the review invokes, such as a custom script or MCP server, is itself waiting on interactive input or an external resource.
The CI runner's timeout is set too low for large PRs, which is what makes certain review jobs appear to hang.
-p requires a companion --non-interactive flag to suppress permission prompts, and this job is missing it.

rationale.correct: Once -p correctly puts Claude Code itself into non-interactive mode, a persistent hang is more likely coming from something Claude Code calls out to — a tool, script, or external service still waiting on input or a slow/blocked resource — independent of Claude Code's own print-mode behavior.

distractors.A: -p is the documented, correct mechanism; abandoning it because a hang persists elsewhere misdiagnoses the cause.
distractors.C: A too-low timeout would cause the job to fail fast, not hang indefinitely — that's the opposite symptom.
distractors.D: There is no separate required companion flag; -p is the complete non-interactive invocation.

scenario: A CI review currently posts inline comments using --output-format json and --json-schema. The team wants to add a new confidence field to every finding without breaking the existing downstream parser that only recognizes the original fields.
stem: What is the safest way to introduce the new field?

options.text: Add confidence as a new optional field in the JSON schema, and update the downstream parser to read it while tolerating its absence.
Remove --json-schema entirely so the new field can be added freely without schema validation rejecting the output.
Post two separate sets of findings — one with the old schema, one with the new — and let the downstream code pick whichever it prefers.
Rename the existing fields to make room for the new one, since a JSON object has a fixed number of keys and the schema is full.

rationale.correct: Adding a new field as optional in the schema is backward compatible: existing parsers that don't yet know about confidence are unaffected, since strict schema enforcement continues to guarantee the fields those parsers do expect, while newer parser code can opt in to reading the addition — and, by tolerating its absence, keeps working with any not-yet-updated callers.

distractors.B: Removing schema enforcement reopens the exact reliability problem --json-schema was adopted to solve.
distractors.C: Maintaining two parallel output formats doubles complexity for no benefit over a single backward-compatible schema addition.
distractors.D: JSON objects don't have a fixed key count; renaming existing fields would break every current consumer for no reason.

scenario: A CI review already avoids repeating unaddressed prior findings by passing them into context. Developers now report the reviewer still occasionally re-flags an issue that was, in fact, already fixed in the latest commit.
stem: What refinement addresses this remaining gap?

options.text: Pass the current diff with the prior findings and have the model re-verify each against the latest code, dropping any now resolved.
Stop passing prior findings into context altogether, since stale findings in the prompt are clearly what triggers the re-flagging.
Maintain a separate resolved-issues list that a human updates by hand after every fix and that the reviewer checks before posting comments.
Increase the context window so more history fits, without changing how findings are evaluated against the current diff.

rationale.correct: The remaining gap is that avoiding restatement isn't the same as verifying resolution — the model needs to actually re-check each prior finding against the current diff and confirm whether it still applies, not simply carry it forward unless told otherwise.

distractors.B: Removing prior context reintroduces the original duplicate-comment problem this design was built to solve.
distractors.C: A manually maintained list defeats the purpose of an automated review and adds ongoing human overhead.
distractors.D: More context alone doesn't instruct the model to actively re-verify each finding against the latest diff; that's a prompting/behavior change, not a capacity change.

scenario: A CI-invoked Claude Code review step currently only posts PR comments and always exits 0 (success), even when it finds a critical security issue. The team wants critical findings to actually block the merge, not just be visible as a comment someone might miss.
stem: What is the most direct way to make critical findings block the merge?

options.text: Have the CI step parse the JSON findings for any critical severity and exit non-zero, so the required check fails and blocks the merge.
Rely on developers to notice and act on the PR comment before merging, as they would with any other review feedback.
Increase the review's `max_tokens` so critical findings are described in more detail and are much harder for reviewers to overlook.
Switch the review to plain `-p` text output instead of structured JSON, since prose is more attention-grabbing than a comment.

rationale.correct: Structured output makes severity machine-readable, so the CI step can programmatically check for critical findings and translate that into the one signal CI platforms actually enforce merge-blocking on: the job's exit code, via a required status check.

distractors.B: Relying on developers to notice a comment is exactly the unreliable, easy-to-miss behavior the team wants to eliminate.
distractors.C: More detail in the finding doesn't change whether the CI job's exit code reflects severity.
distractors.D: Switching back to unstructured prose output removes the very severity signal the CI step needs to parse and act on programmatically.

scenario: A review criterion reads: 'Flag a comment whenever the code near it was changed in this PR.' This is explicit and unambiguous, yet the false-positive rate remains high.
stem: What is the actual problem with this criterion?

options.text: It isn't explicit enough; the wording needs to be made even more precise about what counts as "near".
It tests the wrong condition: nearby code changing doesn't mean the comment's claim now contradicts the code.
Explicit criteria are inherently unreliable for comment-staleness checks, regardless of what condition they specify.
The criterion needs a confidence threshold added on top so that low-confidence matches are filtered out.

rationale.correct: Explicitness alone isn't sufficient — the criterion must also target the condition that actually determines correctness. 'Code changed nearby' is a proxy that doesn't test whether the comment is now wrong; a criterion tied to actual contradiction between the comment's claim and the code's behavior is what the check needs.

distractors.A: The wording is already unambiguous; the flaw is which condition it tests, not how precisely it's phrased.
distractors.C: Explicit criteria work when they test the right condition, as established elsewhere in this exam guide; the failure here is a poorly chosen condition, not the approach itself.
distractors.D: A confidence threshold doesn't fix a criterion that's checking the wrong thing in the first place.

scenario: A style-suggestions category was temporarily disabled for a 60% false-positive rate. After adding explicit criteria, a two-week trial on historical PRs shows a 12% false-positive rate.
stem: What should determine whether it's safe to re-enable the category now?

options.text: Re-enable immediately, since dropping from 60% to 12% shows the fix worked and any measured improvement is sufficient.
Compare the new rate against the accurate categories' rates or a team-set threshold, rather than re-enabling on improvement alone.
Never re-enable a category that was ever disabled, since developers' trust in it is unlikely to recover regardless of fixes.
Re-enable it only after removing the other, already-accurate categories, so the trial can isolate the style category's own effect on noise.

rationale.correct: Improvement alone doesn't establish that a rate is now acceptable — the right precondition is comparing the new rate against a concrete bar (the trusted categories' own rates, or an explicit acceptance threshold), not just noting that it went down from where it was.

distractors.A: Improvement without a defined bar for 'good enough' risks re-enabling a still-too-noisy category and re-eroding trust.
distractors.C: A category can legitimately be fixed and re-enabled; treating disablement as permanent discards real remediation work.
distractors.D: Removing the accurate categories has nothing to do with validating whether the fixed category is now trustworthy on its own.

scenario: A security-review criterion says 'flag any use of `eval()`.' The codebase later adds a sandboxed template-rendering library that internally calls a safely-scoped `eval()` as an implementation detail, and the criterion now flags every template render as a security issue.
stem: What is the most direct way to fix this without abandoning the useful parts of the criterion?

options.text: Add an explicit negative example excluding the sandboxed template library's internal `eval()` use.
Remove the `eval()` criterion entirely, since a rule that now produces false positives is no longer trustworthy.
Tell developers to manually dismiss every template-render finding going forward, since the cause is already understood.
Lower the category's severity so the template-render false positives matter less in developers' triage.

rationale.correct: The criterion is still valuable for genuinely risky `eval()` use; the problem is one specific, now-known pattern it shouldn't apply to. An explicit negative example/exception for that pattern keeps flagging genuinely dangerous `eval()` calls while excluding the known-safe one, so the criterion stays precise without discarding its real value.

distractors.B: Removing the criterion entirely loses its ability to catch genuinely dangerous eval() use elsewhere, over one specific known exception.
distractors.C: Manual dismissal treats a fixable criteria gap as an ongoing chore instead of fixing the root cause once.
distractors.D: Lowering severity doesn't stop the false positives from firing — it just makes them quieter noise instead of eliminating them.

scenario: A 'no hard-coded secrets' criterion was written and tuned six months ago. Since then, the team adopted a new config-templating pattern where placeholder strings like `{{DB_PASSWORD}}` appear throughout the codebase — literal template syntax, never an actual secret. The criterion increasingly flags these placeholders as hard-coded secrets.
stem: What does this situation call for, and why?

options.text: Periodic criteria maintenance: update the criterion as codebase patterns evolve, e.g., excluding the template-placeholder syntax.
Nothing — a criterion that was correct when written remains correct forever, regardless of how the codebase evolves.
Immediately disable the entire secrets-detection category, since one new pattern broke it and its results can no longer be trusted.
Retrain developers to stop using the templating pattern, so the existing, well-tuned criterion doesn't need to change.

rationale.correct: Explicit criteria are precise for the codebase as it existed when written; as new legitimate patterns emerge, criteria can drift out of sync and need periodic revisiting and updating, the same way any other project-specific documentation does. Criteria are a maintained asset, not a permanent one-time artifact.

distractors.B: Codebases evolve, and criteria written against yesterday's patterns can become imprecise against today's — treating them as eternally correct is exactly the assumption that causes this drift.
distractors.C: Disabling the whole category over one new pattern is more disruptive than the targeted fix (updating the criterion) actually needed.
distractors.D: Asking the team to abandon a legitimate, useful pattern just to avoid updating a review criterion has the fix backwards.

scenario: You add five few-shot examples to a classification prompt, all drawn from the exact same product category (electronics returns). After deployment, the model classifies electronics returns very accurately but performs poorly on furniture and clothing returns — categories it handled reasonably well before the examples were added.
stem: What is the most likely cause, and the fix?

options.text: The single-category examples taught electronics-specific patterns, not general logic; add examples spanning all the categories.
Few-shot examples always improve every category uniformly; this outcome suggests a bug elsewhere in the pipeline, not the examples.
Adding more examples from the same electronics category will fix the furniture and clothing regressions by reinforcing the logic.
This is expected and unavoidable; few-shot examples can only ever help the specific category they're drawn from.

rationale.correct: When every example is drawn from one narrow slice, the model can pick up patterns specific to that slice rather than the general principle you meant to teach — a form of overfitting to the examples' narrow distribution. Diversifying the examples to represent the actual range of cases is the fix.

distractors.B: This is a known, real risk of few-shot prompting (over-narrow example sets skewing behavior), not evidence of an unrelated bug.
distractors.C: Adding more of the same narrow category would likely make the skew worse, not better.
distractors.D: Few-shot examples can generalize well when they're representative of the range of cases — the problem here is the narrow, unrepresentative set, not an inherent limitation.

scenario: A customer-support agent's replies are technically correct but read as curt and impersonal; the team wants a warmer, more empathetic tone without changing what information is actually communicated.
stem: What is the most effective way to establish this tone consistently?

options.text: Provide a few worked example replies in the target voice that acknowledge the customer's situation, then give the same information.
Add the instruction 'be warm and empathetic' to the system prompt and nothing else, since the information content is already correct.
Increase the model's temperature so replies sound more natural and varied instead of templated, stiff, and repetitive.
Shorten every reply, since brevity is what reads as impersonal when customers are already frustrated.

rationale.correct: Tone, like format or classification boundaries, is something few-shot examples convey more reliably than an adjective in a prompt — concrete worked examples show the model exactly what 'warmer' looks like in practice, in a way abstract instructions don't. The examples should acknowledge the customer's situation, then give the same information warmly.

distractors.B: A bare adjective like 'warm' is exactly the kind of vague instruction that tends to be interpreted inconsistently, the same failure mode as vague review criteria.
distractors.C: Higher temperature increases output variability, not adherence to a specific desired tone.
distractors.D: Length isn't necessarily the actual driver of the curt, impersonal feeling; shortening replies further could make it worse, not better.

scenario: You've added eight well-chosen few-shot examples to a document-classification prompt, spanning the range of document types. Accuracy on genuinely ambiguous documents is still poor, and you suspect the issue isn't the prompt at all, but that the task requires domain knowledge (obscure regulatory terminology) the model simply doesn't reliably have.
stem: What does this situation suggest about few-shot prompting's role here?

options.text: Examples teach how to apply judgment the model has, not facts it lacks; for a knowledge gap, supply the knowledge in context instead.
The fix is to add more few-shot examples, since broader coverage of ambiguous documents is what ultimately improves accuracy on those documents.
This means few-shot prompting has failed and should be abandoned for the whole prompt, including the parts that were working well.
Increasing the number of examples to 20+ will eventually compensate for missing domain knowledge by covering more ambiguous cases.

rationale.correct: Few-shot examples are best suited to showing the model how to apply reasoning/judgment it already has — output format, disambiguation logic, tone. When the actual gap is missing factual/domain knowledge, more examples of the same kind won't supply what's missing; the fix is providing that knowledge directly.

distractors.B: Adding more examples doesn't address a knowledge gap, only a reasoning/format gap — more coverage of ambiguous cases can't supply facts the model doesn't have.
distractors.C: The parts of the prompt already working (the well-chosen existing examples handling non-ambiguous cases) shouldn't be discarded just because one sub-problem needs a different fix.
distractors.D: Piling on more examples doesn't inject domain knowledge the model doesn't have; it's the wrong lever for this specific gap.

scenario: You're writing few-shot examples to teach an agent when to escalate a support ticket to a human versus handle it directly. All four examples you drafted are clear-cut 'definitely escalate' cases; none show a case that's handled directly, and none show a borderline case near the actual decision boundary.
stem: What is the most likely shortcoming of this example set, and the fix?

options.text: The examples don't span the decision boundary; add contrasting 'handle directly' cases and a borderline close call.
The example set is already sufficient, since more escalate-cases will make the model more cautious, which is the safer outcome.
The fix is to add ten more 'definitely escalate' examples to reinforce the pattern further and make escalation more consistent.
Few-shot examples cannot teach a boundary decision like this one at all; explicit if/then rules are needed to define it.

rationale.correct: Examples teach by contrast — a set that only shows one side of a decision (always escalate) gives the model no signal about where the boundary actually is or what a 'handle directly' case looks like. Representative examples need to span the decision, including a genuinely close call, not cluster on one outcome.

distractors.B: Reinforcing only one side of the decision doesn't make the model more accurate at a boundary; it can bias it toward over-escalating even clear-cut direct-handle cases.
distractors.C: More examples of the same one-sided type doesn't add the missing contrast the boundary decision needs.
distractors.D: Few-shot examples are a well-established technique for teaching exactly this kind of boundary/disambiguation judgment, provided they're constructed to actually span it.

scenario: A pipeline uses tool_use with a JSON schema requiring line_items to be a non-empty array of {sku, quantity} objects. Extractions are always syntactically valid JSON conforming to that shape, yet some invoices come back with zero line items even though the source document clearly lists several.
stem: What does this indicate, and is it addressed by tool_use's schema guarantee?

options.text: Since output is always schema-valid, this is not a problem tool_use can address at all, and nothing further should be done.
The schema guarantees structural validity, not complete contents; this semantic completeness gap needs its own check.
The schema itself is broken and must be rewritten to require a minimum array length before this can be diagnosed.
Switching to a larger model will resolve completeness regardless of the schema, since smaller models skip line items.

rationale.correct: tool_use enforces structural conformance — the array's shape is valid — but has no way to guarantee the array's contents are complete or correct. Missing line items despite a valid empty (or under-filled) array is a semantic completeness problem, which needs an explicit downstream check, not a schema-shape fix. For example, validate the line-item count against other invoice fields.

distractors.A: The gap is real and addressable — just not through the schema-conformance mechanism alone; a completeness check is the appropriate addition.
distractors.C: A minimum-length constraint could force a non-empty array but wouldn't guarantee the array's contents are the correct items — it would risk the model padding with placeholder values instead.
distractors.D: Model size doesn't address a structural/procedural gap in what's being validated; a completeness check does.

scenario: An invoice_number field is present on most invoices but genuinely absent on a minority of internal transfer documents. When present, it must always match the pattern INV-\d{6}.
stem: How should the schema be designed to prevent both fabrication and format drift?

options.text: Require the field always, format-constrained, forcing the model to invent a plausible-looking value for the documents that lack one.
Make the field nullable, with the format pattern applied only to non-null values, so absence is representable and present values must conform.
Make the field a free-text string with no pattern constraint, to avoid ever rejecting a real but unusually-formatted value.
Drop the field from the schema entirely, since it isn't present on every document type and a partial field complicates downstream validation.

rationale.correct: Nullable handles genuine absence without fabrication pressure, and a format constraint that only applies to non-null values preserves that the field's shape is guaranteed whenever it actually exists — combining both concerns rather than trading one off against the other.

distractors.A: Requiring the field forces exactly the fabrication this design is meant to prevent, for the documents that legitimately lack one.
distractors.C: Dropping the format constraint entirely lets genuinely malformed values through even when the field is present, undermining downstream use of the field.
distractors.D: Removing the field entirely discards a field that IS meaningful and extractable on the majority of documents that do have it.

scenario: Beyond document_type (five known values plus new/ambiguous cases), each document also needs a sub_category whose valid values depend on which document_type was assigned, and new sub-categories appear even more often than new document types.
stem: How should the schema handle the dependent, even-more-volatile sub_category field?

options.text: Use the same enum-plus-other-plus-unclear pattern for sub_category as for document_type, independent of the two fields' different volatility.
Keep the other-with-detail fallback, expect it to fire more often, and use document_type as context for interpreting the other value.
Make sub_category a required field with no fallback at all, since it's clearly the more important and more specific of the two fields.
Merge document_type and sub_category into a single combined enum listing every valid pairing in advance, so dependencies are explicit.

rationale.correct: The same extensible pattern still applies, but recognizing that sub_category is more volatile means expecting the fallback path to carry more real cases, and using the already-known document_type as context to interpret an 'other' sub_category avoids trying to pre-enumerate every future pairing. Document_type is treated as authoritative context, rather than requiring sub_category's enum to anticipate every combination up front.

distractors.A: Applying the pattern identically without accounting for the different volatility and the dependency between the two fields misses the actual design challenge in this scenario.
distractors.C: A required field with no fallback for the more volatile of the two fields is the fabrication-risk pattern this whole approach exists to avoid.
distractors.D: Pre-enumerating every valid pairing defeats the purpose of an extensible design for a field that changes more often than the other.

scenario: A payment-extraction schema needs a `payment_method` object whose actual shape differs by type: a credit card needs `last_four` and `expiry`; a bank transfer needs `routing_number` and `account_last_four`; digital wallets need just a `provider_name`.
stem: What is the most robust way to model this in the schema?

options.text: Use a discriminated structure: a `type` enum of the three payment methods, with each type requiring only its own fields, so a card entry can't carry a routing number.
Make every possible field (last_four, expiry, routing_number, account_last_four, provider_name) available and optional on one flat object, with no connection between them and the type.
Use three completely separate top-level schemas and have the model guess which one to use with no field indicating which was chosen.
Store the payment method details as a single free-text string, since the fields vary too much to model formally.

rationale.correct: A discriminated type — a type field paired with type-appropriate required fields — captures the real constraint that each payment method has its own valid shape, preventing nonsensical combinations (like a wallet entry carrying a routing number) while still keeping the output fully structured and validated.

distractors.B: A flat object with every field optional and no connection to type allows invalid combinations (e.g., a credit card entry with a routing number) and gives downstream code no reliable way to know which fields are actually meaningful.
distractors.C: Separate schemas with no indicator of which was used forces downstream code to guess the shape, defeating the purpose of structured output.
distractors.D: A free-text string discards the very structure and validation that make this data reliably usable downstream.

scenario: Your extraction schema defines `invoice_total` as a number, but the model sometimes returns it as the string "$1,240.00" instead of the numeric value 1240.00, even though the surrounding fields validate fine.
stem: What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Add explicit normalization guidance plus a worked input/output example that strips symbols and commas and coerces to a number.
Loosen the schema so `invoice_total` accepts either a string or a number, and normalize downstream in application code.
Reject the whole extraction and ask a human to retype the number, so no malformed value reaches the ledger.
Increase `max_tokens` so the model has more room to format the number correctly instead of truncating it.

rationale.correct: This is a formatting/normalization issue the model can reliably fix once shown exactly what's expected — a concrete input/output example demonstrating the currency-string-to-number transformation is the most direct, low-effort fix.

distractors.B: Loosening the schema to accept either type pushes the normalization problem downstream instead of fixing it, and reintroduces exactly the inconsistency structured extraction is meant to eliminate.
distractors.C: Discarding a mostly-correct extraction over one fixable formatting issue is disproportionate.
distractors.D: More tokens doesn't address a formatting/type convention the model simply hasn't been shown clearly.

scenario: An extraction attempt fails validation for two independent reasons at once: a malformed date and a missing required field that genuinely is present in the source document.
stem: How should the retry-with-error-feedback request be constructed?

options.text: Send only the date error first, then retry a second time for the missing field once the date is fixed, one issue per retry.
Include both validation errors in one retry request, with the original document and failed output, so the model fixes both in one pass.
Discard the attempt and skip straight to human review, since two simultaneous errors suggest the case is too complex for retry to fix reliably.
Retry with the date error only, and silently drop the missing-required-field error since it will likely resolve on its own.

rationale.correct: Since both are independent, fixable, structural/format issues, surfacing both validation errors together in one retry lets the model correct them in a single pass — sequencing them across separate retries adds unnecessary round-trips for problems that don't depend on each other.

distractors.A: Splitting genuinely independent, fixable errors across sequential retries costs an extra round-trip for no benefit.
distractors.C: Two structural errors are still within retry-with-feedback's wheelhouse; escalating to human review is premature when both are correctable format/completeness issues.
distractors.D: Silently dropping a real validation error risks shipping data that's still wrong; it should be surfaced, not ignored.

scenario: An extraction pipeline processes only page 1 of a multi-page contract PDF. The governing_law field is required and comes back null, but the clause actually appears on page 3.
stem: Is this the same 'retry won't help' situation as information that is genuinely absent from the source, or something else?

options.text: The same situation — retries never help with a missing field, regardless of cause, so the fix is to make the field nullable and move on.
A different situation — the clause exists in the source but was never supplied to the model; include page 3 in the extraction input and resubmit.
The same situation — given page 1, the model correctly reported the field as absent, and since that is what the document showed it, more input wouldn't change the answer.
A different situation, but unfixable — multi-page contracts should be excluded from extraction entirely.

rationale.correct: This differs from true absence: the data exists in the source, it just wasn't included in what the model was given. Unlike a field that's genuinely missing from the document, this is fixed by supplying the missing page, not by accepting null or escalating to a human — once page 3 is in the input, a retry (or the original request resubmitted with full input) can succeed.

distractors.A: This isn't the genuinely-absent case; treating it identically would accept a null that a fuller input could actually resolve.
distractors.C: The model didn't determine anything about page 3 at all — it was never given that page, which is different from having reviewed the full document and finding no such clause.
distractors.D: Excluding an entire document category is a disproportionate response to an input-scoping bug that has a direct fix.

scenario: An extraction pipeline retries with error feedback on validation failures. For one particularly messy scanned document, the model has now failed validation on three consecutive attempts, each time producing a different but still-invalid result.
stem: What should happen at this point?

options.text: Cap retries at a small, fixed number of attempts and route the document to a human for review.
Keep retrying indefinitely with the same error feedback, since each new attempt gives the model another chance to land on valid output.
Silently accept the third attempt's output even though it fails validation, since three attempts is 'enough effort' and the result is probably close.
Switch to a completely different extraction schema after each failed attempt, hoping one eventually validates.

rationale.correct: Retry-with-feedback is effective for correctable format/structural mistakes, but a pattern of repeated, differently-invalid attempts on the same document suggests the document itself is unusually difficult, not a quick, fixable mistake — capping retries and escalating to a human avoids burning unbounded attempts on a case that likely needs one anyway.

distractors.B: Indefinite retrying on a document that's already failed three distinct ways risks never terminating while providing no better guarantee of eventual success.
distractors.C: Accepting invalid output because enough attempts were made abandons the validation guarantee entirely for this document.
distractors.D: Swapping schemas per attempt doesn't address why extraction is failing and makes the failure pattern harder to diagnose, not easier.

scenario: A third workflow generates a weekly summary digest emailed to stakeholders every Monday morning; the job currently starts Sunday night and nobody is waiting on it in real time, but stakeholders do expect it delivered reliably by a specific hour.
stem: Is this workflow a good fit for the Message Batches API, alongside the already-agreed overnight report?

options.text: No — any deadline at all, even a next-morning one with slack, disqualifies a workflow from batch processing, since delivery time can't be guaranteed.
Yes — no one is waiting on it interactively, and submitting with enough lead time for batch's up-to-24-hour window meets the Monday deadline.
Yes, but only if the batch is submitted at the exact moment the deadline begins, regardless of the up-to-24-hour processing window.
No — weekly-cadence jobs are never appropriate for the Batches API, regardless of latency tolerance.

rationale.correct: The relevant distinction is whether anyone is blocked waiting on the result in real time, not the mere existence of a deadline. Submitted with enough lead time relative to batch's up-to-24-hour window, this latency-tolerant, non-interactive workflow fits the same profile as the already-agreed overnight report.

distractors.A: A deadline with slack is exactly what batch handles well; it's tight, blocking deadlines that are the disqualifying case.
distractors.C: Submitting right at the deadline ignores the up-to-24-hour window and risks missing the delivery time; lead time is required, not optional.
distractors.D: Cadence (weekly vs. nightly) isn't the deciding factor; latency tolerance and the absence of a blocking wait are.

scenario: In a batch of 500 jobs, 12 fail due to oversized documents (fixable by chunking) and 3 fail because the source PDF is corrupted and won't open at all.
stem: How should the recovery differ between these two failure groups?

options.text: Treat all 15 identically: chunk every failed document and resubmit all 15 using their custom_ids, keeping recovery to a single code path.
Chunk and resubmit the 12 oversized documents; re-source the 3 corrupted files (or flag them for manual attention) before resubmitting them.
Discard all 15 failures and accept the loss, since any failure in a large batch is expected.
Resubmit the entire batch of 500, since distinguishing failure types adds unnecessary complexity.

rationale.correct: The two failure types need different remediation: chunking fixes an oversized-but-otherwise-valid document, but a corrupted file has no valid content to chunk — it needs a new source file (or human attention) before resubmission is even possible. custom_id still lets you target exactly these 15 without touching the 485 that succeeded.

distractors.A: Chunking a corrupted file that won't open produces nothing usable; the two failure classes need genuinely different fixes.
distractors.C: Discarding recoverable failures (the 12 oversized ones, at least) wastes work that a straightforward fix would have salvaged.
distractors.D: Resubmitting all 500 wastes cost reprocessing 485 jobs that already succeeded, and still wouldn't fix the corrupted files.

scenario: You submit a single Message Batch containing 1,000 requests. You need the results for 20 specific, urgent requests within that batch back faster than the rest, but the whole batch is one submission.
stem: What does the Message Batches API let you do here?

options.text: Nothing within the batch — there is no intra-batch ordering; submit the 20 urgent requests separately (sync calls or a small batch).
Set a `priority` field on those 20 requests so the batch scheduler processes them ahead of the other 980 requests in the same submission.
The batch API automatically detects which requests are most urgent from their content and schedules those first.
Set a shorter `processing_window` on the batch so all 1,000 requests, including the 20 urgent ones, must finish sooner.

rationale.correct: The Message Batches API doesn't offer intra-batch prioritization — genuinely urgent items shouldn't be mixed into a large batch alongside non-urgent ones if they need to come back faster; separating them into their own submission (sync calls or a smaller, dedicated batch) is the correct way to get differentiated timing.

distractors.B: There's no such priority field for reordering processing within a single batch submission.
distractors.C: The API doesn't infer urgency from request content; it has no concept of relative priority within a batch.
distractors.D: There is no configurable processing window. A batch completes within up to 24 hours, and nothing lets you shorten that for the batch or for individual requests inside it.

scenario: A team processes 50 documents a day through a synchronous pipeline. Someone proposes switching to the Message Batches API for its 50% cost savings, even though the workload has no latency tolerance — results are needed within seconds for an interactive tool.
stem: Is this a good use of the Message Batches API?

options.text: No — batch has no guaranteed latency SLA (results can take up to 24 hours), which a seconds-latency interactive tool can't tolerate.
Yes — 50% savings is worth pursuing for any workload, regardless of latency requirements, since cost reduction is the primary consideration.
Yes, as long as the team polls very frequently, since frequent polling effectively restores real-time behavior.
No, but only because 50 documents a day is too small a volume for the Batches API to apply to at all.

rationale.correct: Batch's savings come paired with no latency guarantee (processing can take up to 24 hours); a workload that genuinely needs results within seconds for interactive use is fundamentally incompatible with that trade-off, regardless of how attractive the cost savings look in isolation.

distractors.B: Cost savings alone don't justify batch when the latency trade-off is incompatible with the actual requirement; the workload's needs, not just cost, determine fit.
distractors.C: Polling frequency doesn't change how quickly the batch itself is processed; it only affects how soon you notice it's done, which is irrelevant if the underlying processing time itself is too slow.
distractors.D: Volume isn't the disqualifying factor here — even at high volume, this same workload would still be latency-incompatible with batch; the real issue is the interactive, seconds-scale requirement.

scenario: A team's code-review prompt for self-review already says, in bold, 'Be maximally critical and assume there are bugs, even if the code looks correct to you.' The same session still misses the same class of bugs it introduced.
stem: Why does strengthening the self-review instruction not fix this?

options.text: The instruction wasn't strong enough; an even more emphatic version, repeated at the end of the prompt, would resolve it.
Wording isn't the issue — the session retains the reasoning that produced the code, which makes it less likely to challenge its own decisions.
This means self-review should never be attempted in any form.
The instruction needs to be moved from the user prompt into the system prompt, where behavioral directives carry more weight, to take effect.

rationale.correct: No amount of emphatic wording changes what the model already has in context — its own generation reasoning, which it still treats as settled. The fix that actually addresses this is an independent review instance without that inherited context, not a stronger version of the same in-session instruction.

distractors.A: Escalating the wording doesn't change the underlying cause (retained context), so it wouldn't be expected to help regardless of emphasis.
distractors.C: Self-review isn't useless — it's just insufficient as a substitute for a genuinely independent instance; the guide doesn't recommend abandoning review, it recommends restructuring it.
distractors.D: Prompt placement doesn't remove the retained reasoning context that's the actual limitation here.

scenario: A team added a cross-file integration pass on top of their per-file passes, but it still misses a bug where one file's function signature change silently breaks a caller in another file, because the integration pass is currently just re-running the same per-file prompt across all files at once.
stem: What is missing from the integration pass as currently implemented?

options.text: Nothing; simply running the per-file prompt across all files together already constitutes a correct integration pass.
A distinct focus of its own: reasoning about cross-file data flow and contracts, such as changed signatures and their call sites.
The fix is to increase the model's context window so all files fit even more comfortably and each caller stays in view.
The fix is to run the per-file pass a second time on every file, in addition to the first pass, to catch what the first run missed.

rationale.correct: An integration pass that just reruns the per-file prompt across more files at once still asks the same local questions, not the cross-file question. It needs a distinct prompt/focus specifically on data flow and contracts between files to catch the kind of signature-change bug described.

distractors.A: Running the same local-focused prompt at a wider scope doesn't introduce reasoning about cross-file contracts, which is exactly what's missing.
distractors.C: A larger context window doesn't itself introduce cross-file reasoning if the prompt never asks for it.
distractors.D: Repeating the same per-file prompt a second time doesn't add the missing focus; it just repeats the same local-scope analysis.

scenario: A team already runs three review passes (per-file, cross-file integration, and independent-instance verification) and is considering adding a fourth: a dedicated 'style consistency' pass on top. Review turnaround time is already a common developer complaint.
stem: What should the team weigh before adding a fourth pass?

options.text: Whether it catches a distinct class of issue the existing three miss, weighed against the added turnaround time developers already complain about.
Nothing — more review passes always improve quality with no meaningful downside, so it should be added unconditionally.
The fourth pass should replace one of the existing three, regardless of what each currently catches, simply to keep the total pass count the same.
Turnaround time complaints are irrelevant to review-architecture decisions and shouldn't factor into this at all.

rationale.correct: Each review pass in a multi-pass architecture should target a genuinely distinct failure mode; adding passes has a real cost in turnaround time, so a new pass is worth adding only when it catches something the existing ones don't, weighed against a complaint that's already live.

distractors.B: More passes come with real turnaround-time cost; treating additional passes as free ignores the tradeoff the team is already feeling.
distractors.C: Swapping passes without considering what each existing pass actually catches risks losing real coverage for no principled reason.
distractors.D: Developer-experience costs like turnaround time are a legitimate input to a review-architecture decision, not something to ignore.

scenario: A team runs a per-file review pass and a cross-file integration pass. Currently, the integration pass runs first, before any per-file findings exist, and it has to re-derive basic per-file context from scratch to do its cross-file analysis.
stem: What is the most likely improvement from reordering these two passes?

options.text: Per-file passes run first and feed their findings in, so the integration pass builds on established local context instead of re-deriving it.
Pass order has no effect on either pass's effectiveness; the two are entirely independent regardless of sequencing.
The integration pass should always run before per-file passes, since cross-file issues are inherently higher priority than local ones.
Both passes should be merged into a single combined pass that reviews each file and its cross-file links together, eliminating the ordering question.

rationale.correct: The integration pass's job — reasoning about relationships across files — benefits from having each file's local findings already established, rather than re-deriving that local context itself; sequencing per-file first lets the integration pass build on that groundwork instead of duplicating it.

distractors.B: The passes aren't fully independent when one's output (per-file findings) is useful groundwork for the other; order can matter for efficiency and grounding.
distractors.C: Priority of issue type doesn't determine a mechanical requirement about which pass must run first; the actual consideration is what context each pass needs to do its job well.
distractors.D: Merging back into one combined pass reintroduces the exact attention-dilution problem separate per-file and integration passes were designed to solve.

scenario: A case-facts block correctly preserves exact amounts, dates, and order numbers across a long conversation, but after many issues accumulate in one extended case, the block itself has grown large enough to consume a meaningful share of the context budget.
stem: What is the appropriate way to keep the case-facts block itself from becoming a new context problem?

options.text: Let it keep growing indefinitely, since case facts must never be dropped once captured, regardless of how large the block becomes.
Periodically prune facts no longer tied to any open issue, such as a closed sub-issue's specifics, while protecting facts for open concerns.
Move the case-facts block into the conversation history itself, so it gets summarized along with everything else.
Cap the case-facts block at a fixed small size and drop the oldest facts first, regardless of whether they're still relevant to an open issue.

rationale.correct: The case-facts block's value is precision on facts that still matter; once a sub-issue is fully resolved, its specifics are no longer load-bearing and can be pruned, keeping the block's growth tied to genuinely open concerns rather than an ever-accumulating, unbounded record.

distractors.A: Unbounded growth defeats the purpose of a lean, precise persistent block and recreates a context-budget problem of its own.
distractors.C: Moving the facts into the summarized history reintroduces exactly the lossy-summarization risk the block was created to avoid.
distractors.D: A naive oldest-first cap risks dropping facts still tied to a currently open issue, purely based on age rather than relevance.

scenario: A single agent process handles support conversations for many customers concurrently. A bug causes one customer's case-facts (order number, amount) to appear in a different customer's conversation history.
stem: What is the most direct fix?

options.text: Strictly isolate each conversation's context (history, case-facts block) per session, with nothing shared or pooled across concurrent conversations.
Summarize more aggressively so any leaked facts are compressed and less noticeable.
Add a case-facts block to every conversation, since the block itself prevents cross-contamination by keeping each customer's facts in one labeled place.
Increase the context window so there's room for multiple customers' facts without conflict.

rationale.correct: Cross-conversation leakage is a strict isolation failure, not a size or compression problem — each conversation's context must be kept entirely separate per session, with no shared state that could let one customer's facts bleed into another's history.

distractors.B: Compressing leaked facts still leaves them present in the wrong conversation; it doesn't fix the isolation failure that caused the leak.
distractors.C: A case-facts block preserves facts precisely; it does nothing to enforce separation between different conversations' contexts.
distractors.D: A bigger window doesn't isolate anything — it just makes room for more data, which doesn't prevent it from being routed to the wrong conversation.

scenario: A support agent's context window has a hard 8,000-token budget for conversation history. A very long, multi-issue case has accumulated 15,000 tokens of raw history and is about to exceed the budget.
stem: What is the most effective way to stay within budget without losing what matters?

options.text: Keep the case-facts block and a concise summary of resolved context, and summarize or drop the lowest-value raw turns first.
Truncate the oldest turns until the token count fits, regardless of what they contain, since recent turns matter most to the next reply.
Truncate the newest turns until the token count fits, keeping only the earliest history where the case was originally set up.
Refuse to continue the conversation once the raw history exceeds the budget.

rationale.correct: A hard budget forces a choice about what to keep; the right one prioritizes the load-bearing precise facts (exact amounts, order numbers, dates, commitments) and a compact summary over verbose raw turns, rather than an indiscriminate cut from the start or end that could just as easily remove the case-facts as any other content.

distractors.B: Truncating strictly by age can just as easily remove important early facts (like the original case-facts) as unimportant chatter — it isn't a targeted way to protect what matters.
distractors.C: Dropping the newest turns removes the most recent, often most relevant, context of the conversation.
distractors.D: Refusing to continue abandons the conversation instead of managing the budget with the tools already available (summarization, prioritized retention).

scenario: A customer starts a support conversation in live chat, then the case is handed off to a phone agent (a different system) who has no access to the chat transcript, only whatever gets explicitly passed along.
stem: What should be passed to the phone agent to preserve context across this channel switch?

options.text: A structured handoff summary — customer ID, core case facts, root cause, and commitments already made — rather than the raw chat transcript.
Nothing — the phone agent should start the conversation from scratch and ask the customer to repeat everything.
The full raw chat transcript, since more information is always better regardless of the receiving system and nothing gets lost in translation.
Only the customer's name, since the phone agent can look up everything else themselves.

rationale.correct: The same principle that governs handoffs within one system applies across a channel switch: a structured summary of the load-bearing facts (identity, root cause, amounts, commitments) gives the receiving agent what they need to act, without requiring them to parse a raw transcript in a different system or make the customer repeat themselves.

distractors.B: Starting from scratch and re-asking everything degrades the customer experience and discards work already done.
distractors.C: A raw transcript dumped into a different system and workflow is unstructured and slow to use, the same problem structured handoffs solve within one system.
distractors.D: A bare name omits the substantive facts (root cause, amounts, commitments) the phone agent actually needs to continue the case.

scenario: A customer's message reads: 'I want to talk to a person, not a bot — also, can you tell me the status of order #4471 while I wait?'
stem: How should the agent interpret the second half of the message?

options.text: As evidence the customer doesn't actually need escalation, since they're willing to interact with the agent for the order-status question.
As a quick lookup while waiting — the escalation request stands, so route to a human, optionally after giving the order status.
As a cancellation of the earlier escalation request, since any further engagement with the agent implicitly withdraws it.
As grounds to ask the customer to clarify whether they still want a human, before doing anything else.

rationale.correct: The explicit request for a human is still the operative signal; a customer can want a quick answer while waiting without that retracting their stated preference. Escalation should proceed, and providing the order status is a reasonable courtesy alongside it, not a substitute for honoring the request.

distractors.A: Willingness to ask one more question doesn't retract an explicit, first-class escalation trigger already stated in the same message.
distractors.C: Nothing in the message actually withdraws the escalation request; treating continued engagement as automatic withdrawal isn't supported by what the customer said.
distractors.D: Asking the customer to reconfirm an already-explicit request adds friction the guide specifically warns against.

scenario: The agent acknowledges a customer's frustration about a damaged order and offers to process a reshipment now. The customer replies: 'Fine, but this had better not happen a fourth time,' without asking for a human.
stem: What should the agent do at this point?

options.text: Escalate now, since the customer's continued frustration after the first acknowledgment is itself a stronger signal than before.
Proceed with the reshipment as offered, since the customer accepted it and hasn't asked for a human; frustration alone isn't grounds to escalate.
Ask the customer a second time whether they'd prefer a human, since their tone hasn't improved.
Apply a service credit automatically, since repeated frustration justifies compensation regardless of what was offered or requested.

rationale.correct: The customer accepted the offered resolution and still hasn't asked for a human; persistent frustration on its own remains distinct from an escalation trigger. The agent should proceed with the accepted reshipment rather than treating tone as grounds to escalate or add unrequested friction.

distractors.A: Escalation triggers are explicit requests, policy gaps, or exhausted capability — not the intensity or persistence of frustration by itself.
distractors.C: The customer already accepted the offered path; asking again introduces friction the guide cautions against when a resolution was just accepted.
distractors.D: Compensation wasn't requested or established as policy for this situation, and offering it doesn't follow from the interaction as described.

scenario: After a name-only lookup returns three matches, the agent asks for an order number. The customer provides one, but it still matches two of the three original accounts (a shared/family order).
stem: What should the agent do now that one additional identifier didn't fully disambiguate?

options.text: Pick either of the two remaining matches at random, since asking for a second additional identifier would be excessive after already asking once.
Ask for one more distinguishing identifier, such as email or billing zip code, that separates the two remaining candidates.
Escalate to a human immediately, since needing a second round of clarification indicates the case is now too complex for the agent.
Proceed with whichever of the two accounts has the more recent activity, since recency is a reasonable tiebreaker at this point.

rationale.correct: The same principle that applied to the first ambiguity still applies: request another specific identifier that can distinguish between the remaining candidates, rather than guessing. Needing a second clarifying question doesn't change the underlying rule against acting on an unconfirmed match.

distractors.A: A random pick between two still-live candidate accounts is exactly the heuristic-guess risk the original rule exists to prevent.
distractors.C: A second round of clarification is still a proportionate response to genuine ambiguity, not evidence the case exceeds the agent's scope.
distractors.D: Recency still isn't evidence of identity; it was the wrong basis for a decision the first time and remains so on a second ambiguous match.

scenario: A customer writes: 'This company's return policy is honestly kind of confusing, but whatever, I still need to return a $30 item within your normal 30-day window and I have my receipt.' The request is a completely standard return the agent is fully authorized to process, and the customer has not asked for a human or indicated a desire to stop working with the agent.
stem: Should the agent escalate this to a human?

options.text: No — a remark on the policy's clarity isn't an escalation trigger; this standard return is within the agent's authority.
Yes, because any negative comment about the company should be escalated to protect the customer relationship.
Yes, because mentioning confusion about a policy always signals a policy gap requiring escalation.
Yes, out of caution, since escalating unnecessary cases is always the safer default regardless of cost to resolution speed.

rationale.correct: A passing negative opinion about clarity, on an otherwise completely standard and in-scope request, isn't one of the actual escalation triggers — there's no explicit request for a human, no real policy gap (the return itself is squarely covered), no capability limit, and no stall. The proportionate response is to just process the standard return.
